body:
Nothing actionable today: the scanner returned zero cross-platform arbitrage opportunities, and that's the normal state — a genuine mismatch between Kalshi and Polymarket gold contracts is rare, not something to expect every session.

Gold itself has been unusually choppy this week. Gold (GC=F) December futures opened at $4,436.40 per troy ounce on Thursday, September 3, 2026, up 0.5% from Wednesday's closing price, with the metal trading near $4,470.70 that morning on hopes that the latest Iran escalation would stay contained. By Friday, gold was pretty steady at $4,521.40 per troy ounce, having opened at its highest price all week ahead of the August jobs report, while a same-day data feed showed gold falling to $4,432.56 on September 4, down 0.92% from the previous day — a reminder that spot quotes differ by source and timestamp, which matters when comparing to a specific settlement snapshot. The swings track Fed rate-path uncertainty and Middle East tensions: traders now see roughly a 50% probability of a September rate hike, down from about 63% a day earlier, after Fed Governor Waller said he'd favor holding rates steady if inflation keeps easing.

That volatility explains the wide fan of strikes on the board rather than any mispricing. Kalshi's contracts are settle markets — they pay out only on the single spot price at expiry (5pm ET Sept 30, or year-end) — while Polymarket's touch contracts pay out if gold crosses the level at any point during the window. So a Polymarket weekly touch-high at $4,500 pricing near 51-53¢ isn't in tension with a Kalshi year-end $4,500 contract near 51-58¢; they're answering different questions (touch-anytime vs. settle-at-a-moment) over different horizons, which is the mundane explanation for any strike-by-strike gaps a reader might notice on the table.
headline: No arbitrage found between Kalshi and Polymarket gold contracts as prices whipsaw
